b: Striae gravidarum (stretch marks) : Stretching in genetically predisposed women: abdomen, breasts, thighs, buttocks
Linea nigra : Pigmented line from the pubis to the umbilicus (MSH and oestrogen)
Chloasma (melasma) : Blotchy facial pigmentation
Spider naevi and palmar erythema : Raised oestrogen and skin blood flow; normal
Chadwick's sign : Bluish discolouration of vagina and cervix
Temperature — hot in thyrotoxicosis, febrile illness; cold and clammy in shock
Hydration — assess skin turgor (pinch skin)
Pallor — check palms, conjunctiva, tongue
Jaundice — check sclera, posterior tongue, skin
Cyanosis — bluish discolouration; check hands (peripheral) and tongue (central)

qs.q: Which of the following is a common cause of superficial skin infection characterized by hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches, often referred to as 'sun spots' or 'tinea versicolor'?
qs.e: Malassezia globosa (and other Malassezia species) are the causative agents of pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, a superficial mycosis characterized by discolored skin patches, particularly on the trunk and shoulders.

qs.q: A positive tuberculin skin test, with a firm 15 mm diameter dark red area of induration on the forearm, appears 60 hours after injection of purified protein derivative (PPD). This finding is most likely a consequence of which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
qs.e: * The tuberculin skin test relies on an intact cell-mediated immune response. It is positive with prior mycobacterial exposure, so memory T cells are present and can be reactivated.

qs.q: After 5 days of clindamycin treatment for a skin infection, a patient develops diarrhea (10 watery stools/day), severe abdominal pain, and fever. Which of the following organisms would you be concerned about as the causative pathogen of diarrhea?
qs.e: Clindamycin use has been strongly associated with Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) or pseudomembranous colitis. Clindamycin disrupts normal colonic flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins that cause severe diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever.

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman presents with skin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and a polyclonal rise in IgG. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Key triad: lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly + skin rash + polyclonal IgG in an an elderly patient. Treated with chemotherapy or histone deacetylase inhibitors.

qs.q: A patient presents with severe pruritus and psoriasis-like skin plaques. Years later they develop lymph node and bone marrow involvement. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Mycosis fungoides is a chronic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma starting with pruritus and skin plaques, eventually spreading to deeper organs. Treatment is phototherapy.

qs.q: A 50-year-old immunocompromised man receives non-irradiated blood products after bone marrow transplantation. Two weeks later he develops an extensive skin rash, profuse diarrhea, rising liver enzymes, and severe pancytopenia. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute hemolytic reaction to transfused blood
qs.e: Immunocompromised patient + non-irradiated blood + skin rash + diarrhea + liver dysfunction + pancytopenia = transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Donor lymphocytes engraft and attack host tissues. Prevented by irradiating blood products for immunocompromised recipients.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with CLL receives a blood transfusion. Two weeks later he has fever, a maculopapular rash over the trunk, watery diarrhea, and his CBC shows pancytopenia. Skin biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltration with epidermal apoptosis. Most likely complication?
o: Adverse drug reaction to recent antibiotics
qs.e: CLL (immunocompromised) + non-irradiated transfusion + rash + diarrhea + pancytopenia + epidermal apoptosis on biopsy = transfusion-associated GVHD. Unlike bone marrow GVHD, this is almost universally fatal with no effective treatment. Prevention by irradiation is critical.

es.q: A post-mortem liver function test (LFT) panel reveals significantly elevated Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and GGT. Review of the patient's clinical history indicates widespread pruritis and skin xanthomas. What hepatic pathological process is strongly suggested, and name two other expected clinical fe
es.m: These findings strongly suggest cholestasis. Two other expected clinical features include jaundice (often with dark urine) and pale/clay-colored stools. Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins is also common.

es.q: Describe the characteristic histological feature of sarcoidosis and explain the mechanism behind the associated hypercalcemia. Name one associated skin sign.
es.m: Sarcoidosis is histologically characterized by the presence of **noncaseating granulomas** in multiple organs. The hypercalcemia associated with sarcoidosis is caused by the **active production of Vitamin D** (specifically 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) by macrophages within these granulomas, leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption. One associated skin sign is **Erythema nodosum**, typically seen in acute sarcoidosis.

es.q: Describe the key pathological and clinical features of Sarcoidosis, including a common skin manifestation and the mechanism of associated hypercalcemia.
es.m: 1. **Pathological Hallmark:** Sarcoidosis is characterized by the presence of noncaseating granulomas in multiple organs. 2. **Diagnosis:** It is a diagnosis of exclusion. 3. **Skin Manifestation:** Erythema nodosum is a recognized skin sign associated with acute sarcoidosis. 4. **Hypercalcemia Mechanism:** Associated hypercalcemia is caused by active Vitamin D production by macrophages located within the granulomas.

es.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with systemic symptoms, including skin lesions and hypercalcemia, and is subsequently diagnosed with sarcoidosis. a) What is the hallmark histological feature of sarcoidosis? (1 mark) b) Identify a specific skin sign commonly associated with acute sarcoidosis. (1 mark) c
es.m: a) The hallmark histological feature of sarcoidosis is the presence of noncaseating granulomas. (1 mark) b) Erythema nodosum is a specific skin sign commonly associated with acute sarcoidosis. (1 mark) c) Hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis is caused by active Vitamin D production by activated macrophages within the granulomas. These macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption and subsequent hypercalcemia. (3 marks)

ai.summary: The skin (integument) is the largest organ of the body, functioning as a protective barrier, thermoregulator, and sensory organ. It consists of two primary layers: the epidermis and the dermis, resting upon the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis).

sections.p: The skin (integument) is the largest organ of the body, functioning as a protective barrier, thermoregulator, and sensory organ. It consists of two primary layers: the epidermis and the dermis, resting upon the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis).

b: Epidermis: A non-vascularized stratified squamous epithelium. It consists of five layers (strata) in thick skin: corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, and basale. Key cells include keratinocytes, melanocytes (pigment), Langerhans cells (immune), and Merkel cells (touch).

Dermis: A vascularized connective tissue layer providing structural support. It is divided into the superficial papillary dermis (loose connective tissue) and the deep reticular dermis (dense irregular connective tissue containing collagen and elastin).
Hypodermis: Composed of adipose and loose connective tissue; it anchors the skin to underlying fascia.
Hair Follicles: Associated with sebaceous glands and arrector pili muscles.
Glands: Includes sebaceous glands (holocrine secretion of sebum) and sweat glands (eccrine for cooling; apocrine in axillary/anogenital regions).
Nails: Keratinized plates on the dorsal distal phalanges.
Burns: Classified by depth (superficial to full-thickness), affecting fluid balance and infection risk.
Dermatomes: Areas of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve; essential for neurological localization.
Wound Healing: Involves hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling layers.
Stratum lucidum vs Stratum corneum: Lucidum is a thin, clear layer found only in thick skin, whereas corneum is the superficial cornified layer.
Dermal papillae vs Rete ridges: Papillae are upward projections of the dermis, while rete ridges are downward extensions of the epidermis.
Apocrine vs Eccrine glands: Eccrine glands are for thermoregulation body-wide; apocrine glands are larger, limited to specific areas, and open into hair follicles.
Turgor tests in the elderly: Decreased skin elasticity due to aging can mimic dehydration signs even when the patient is euvolemic.
Cyanosis in dark skin: Central cyanosis may be difficult to detect on the skin surface; clinicians must check mucous membranes and nail beds.
Erythema in shock: In dark-skinned patients, inflammation or redness may appear as a subtle darkening or purplish hue rather than bright red.

faq.q: What is the difference between thick and thin skin?
faq.a: Thick skin has a prominent stratum lucidum and lacks hair follicles or sebaceous glands, while thin skin covers most of the body and contains appendages.

faq.q: Which cell layer is responsible for constant regeneration?
faq.a: The stratum basale contains stem cells that undergo mitosis to replace keratinocytes lost at the surface.

faq.q: What provides the primary structural strength of the skin?
faq.a: The dermis, specifically the reticular layer, provides tensile strength due to its dense irregular connective tissue and collagen fibers.
